qs.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a core value in the Department of Pathology's guiding principles?
qs.e: Integrity, alongside professionalism and innovation, forms the core values of the department. Compassion and diligence are not among the officially stated core values.
qs.s: Department Of Pathology — Course Outline: MCQs

qs.q: What core value of the Department of Pathology emphasizes upholding moral and ethical principles?
qs.e: Integrity, professionalism, and innovation are listed as the three core values of the Department of Pathology. Flexibility and speed are not among these official core values.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The Department of Pathology teaches how disease alters normal structure and function, guiding diagnosis and treatment. It links laboratory findings to clinical decisions, essential for all clinicians.

sections.p: Pathology is the study of disease mechanisms, morphologic changes, and laboratory abnormalities that explain a patient’s signs and symptoms.
b: Provides the basis for accurate diagnosis
Links tissue, blood, and molecular findings to clinical presentation

t.b: What tissue abnormality is present? → Confirms neoplasia, inflammation, or degeneration.
What cell line is affected? → Detects anemia, infection, or marrow failure.

sections.p: Severity is graded using disease‑specific staging systems (e.g., TNM for cancer, WHO grades for lymphoma). Staging guides prognosis and therapy intensity.
b: Stage reflects tumor size, nodal spread, metastasis

t.b: What is tumor size and spread? → Determines stage; if unavailable, use clinical exam and basic ultrasound.

sections.p: Causes are grouped as infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, genetic, and environmental. In low‑resource settings, consider HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B, schistosomiasis, and herbal toxins early.
Patients present with organ‑specific signs (e.g., jaundice for liver disease) plus systemic clues like fever, weight loss, or abnormal labs.
Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; if a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative.

t.b: Is renal function impaired? → Elevated indicates acute or chronic kidney injury; if no lab, use urine output and bedside creatinine dipstick.
Is there pulmonary involvement? → Shows infiltrates, effusion, or mass; if unavailable, use clinical exam and pulse oximetry.
Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? → Positive confirms TB; if unavailable, rely on sputum smear and clinical picture.

sections.p: Identify features that signal rapid deterioration or life‑threatening complications.
b: Mass effect from tumor → organ obstruction

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Choose drugs based on efficacy, safety, and local resistance patterns.
b: Antibiotics for bacterial infection (e.g., ceftriaxone for severe sepsis)

sections.p: Monitor response with repeat labs or imaging; prevent recurrence with vaccination, prophylaxis, and lifestyle counseling.
b: Repeat CBC after treatment of anemia
Screen for TB reactivation in HIV patients

sections.p: Conditions that mimic each other clinically or pathologically.
Lab values may be falsely normal or abnormal, leading to diagnostic error.
b: Ferritin can be high in inflammation despite iron deficiency
Serum bilirubin may be normal in early hemolysis
White blood count may be normal in early sepsis

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained high fever with altered mental status
Severe shortness of breath with low oxygen saturation

faq.q: Why is pathology important for clinicians?
faq.a: It explains why patients look sick and tells which treatment will fix the underlying disease.

faq.q: What if a key test is not available?
faq.a: Use clinical signs, bedside tools, and the next best affordable test to approximate the answer.
Staging and grading systems derived from pathology predict survival and help choose treatment intensity.

exam: Explain how a CBC helps differentiate anemia from infection and what each pattern suggests.
Describe the TNM staging system for solid tumours and its impact on management decisions.
List three common infectious causes of granulomatous inflammation in low‑resource settings and how to confirm each.
